incidents.title: Global users, single origin
incidents.brief: Users in Tokyo and New York hit the same app and static assets travel from one origin region.
incidents.constraint: Large assets cross an ocean each time and latency climbs.
incidents.question: What pattern reduces the latency?

choices.label: Serve static assets from CDN edge PoPs near users
choices.resultBody: Static assets and media are now served from PoPs a few ms from users, and origin CPU drops from 35% to 16%. Cost: a CDN bill and a cache-invalidation strategy for every deploy.

choices.label: Upgrade the primary database to a larger instance
choices.resultBody: A larger database adds cost, but the 500 ms comes from static bytes crossing an ocean on every request; p95 even rises to 625 ms during the migration.

choices.label: Point every user at one US-East load balancer endpoint
choices.resultBody: Pointing users at a single US endpoint doesn't move them; their packets still travel over 100 ms each way and p95 stays at 550 ms.

hints: The bottleneck is distance, not CPU.
Heavy files are static.
Move assets to the edge.

culprit.explanation: The origin's access log shows 82% of its bytes are /static files taking ~1.8 s each to reach Tokyo, while the database answers in 6 ms. The latency is distance to a single origin, not load.

wrongNodeFeedback.users: Users are where the delay is felt, but you can't move them. Check what they download, and from where.
wrongNodeFeedback.db: The slow-query alerts are a nightly report. Live queries finish in about 6 ms, far from the 500 ms p95.

users: RUM tokyo: page load p95 3.8 s, 2.4 MB of images per page
RUM new-york: page load p95 0.9 s, same page
RUM tokyo: TTFB 190 ms, image download 1.6 s
db: query p99 6 ms over last 5 min

incidents.title: Mobile product pages pull 9 MB of images
incidents.brief: StyleLoop's product pages are served from a CDN at a 96% hit ratio, yet phones on 4G wait 6.2 s for LCP: each page ships twelve 750 KB desktop-sized PNGs to 390-pixel-wide screens.
incidents.constraint: Merchants upload one high-resolution master per photo and will not produce extra sizes by hand.
incidents.question: What cuts the bytes each phone downloads?

choices.label: Resize and convert images to AVIF/WebP at the edge
choices.resultTitle: Each phone gets a 60 KB image
choices.resultBody: The edge resizes each master to the requested width and negotiates AVIF or WebP from the Accept header, so a page drops from 9 MB to about 900 KB and LCP p95 falls to 1.9 s. Cost: per-variant transform fees and a slightly lower hit ratio because each image now has several cached variants.

choices.label: Lazy-load every product image below the fold
choices.resultBody: Only four images load up front now, but the hero image that defines LCP is still a 750 KB PNG decoded on a small phone, so LCP p95 only improves to 4.8 s.

choices.label: Raise image Cache-Control max-age to a full year
choices.resultBody: Hit ratio creeps from 96% to 97%, but the images were already served from the edge. The slowness is the 9 MB payload over 4G, which a longer TTL does not shrink.

hints: The hit ratio is already 96%; origin is not the slow part.
Compare the pixel width of the images with the width of the screens showing them.
The edge can transform a response before caching it, keyed by width and format.

incidents.title: Homepage hit ratio collapses to 11%
incidents.brief: After a framework upgrade, NewsDeck's origin started sending Vary: User-Agent on the homepage. The CDN now stores a copy per browser string, about 9,000 variants, and origin load jumped from 1,500 to 14,000 req/s.
incidents.constraint: The homepage really does differ between mobile and desktop layouts; serving one layout to everyone breaks phones.
incidents.question: How do you keep separate layouts without 9,000 cache copies?

choices.label: Normalize User-Agent into three device classes in the key
choices.resultBody: An edge rule maps each User-Agent to mobile, tablet or desktop, sets a device-class header and varies on that instead, so every PoP holds three copies and hit ratio returns to 94%. Cost: the edge's UA-parsing rules must be maintained as new devices appear.

choices.label: Strip the Vary: User-Agent header at the edge entirely
choices.resultBody: Hit ratio jumps to 97%, but whichever layout was cached first is served to everyone. Within minutes phones in half the PoPs render the desktop homepage and mobile bounce rate doubles.

choices.label: Buy four times more edge cache storage per PoP
choices.resultBody: Storage was never the limit: each of the 9,000 variants is requested only a few times per TTL, so they miss regardless of disk size. Hit ratio moves from 11% to 14%.

hints: Look at what the origin started adding to its response headers.
How many distinct values does that header's input really have that matter to the page?
Collapse the input to a few buckets before it reaches the cache key.

incidents.title: Patch day sends 60 Gbps straight to origin
incidents.brief: RiftForge ships a 24 GB game patch to 3 million players. Hit ratio for the patch is 0%: the CDN will not cache objects over 20 GB, so every download streams from origin at 60 Gbps.
incidents.constraint: The origin uplink is 80 Gbps and patch day traffic keeps climbing for 48 hours.
incidents.question: How do you get the patch cached at the edge?

choices.label: Split the patch into 256 MB chunks via a manifest
choices.resultBody: The launcher downloads a manifest and then about 94 chunks of 256 MB, each well under the size limit, so PoPs cache them after the first request and origin egress drops to ~2 Gbps. Bonus: failed downloads resume per chunk. Cost: a launcher update and a manifest step in the build pipeline.

choices.label: Set a 30-day Cache-Control TTL on the 24 GB patch file
choices.resultBody: The header is honored only for objects the CDN is willing to store. A 24 GB file is still over the 20 GB limit, so every download keeps passing through to origin at about 61 Gbps.

choices.label: Add an origin shield tier between the PoPs and origin
choices.resultTitle: The shield passes it through too
choices.resultBody: The shield is the same CDN with the same object-size limit, so it proxies the 24 GB file uncached. Every download now takes an extra hop and origin egress stays near 60 Gbps.

hints: A 0% hit ratio on a file everyone wants means the CDN is refusing to store it.
Check the CDN's limits, not the TTL.
What if the file the CDN sees were much smaller?

incidents.title: Campaign launch floods origin with landing-page misses
incidents.brief: PayFlow's email campaign links to /pricing?utm_source=mail&utm_campaign=q3&uid=... with a unique uid per recipient. The CDN keys on the full URL, so 2.4 million clicks produce 2.4 million cache misses; origin runs at 93% CPU.
incidents.constraint: The page does use ?lang= to choose a translation, and marketing needs the utm values in analytics.
incidents.question: How do you make those clicks hit the edge cache?

choices.label: Build the cache key from path and ?lang= only
choices.resultBody: The edge builds the key from the path and ?lang= alone, so every recipient in the same language shares one cached page and hit ratio climbs to 97%. The browser still sees the full URL, so analytics reads utm values client-side. Cost: any new meaningful parameter must be added to the allowlist.

choices.label: Ignore every query string in the edge cache key
choices.resultBody: Hit ratio is excellent, but ?lang= is ignored too, so each PoP serves whichever translation it cached first. Support tickets about wrong-language pricing pages arrive within ten minutes.

choices.label: Autoscale the marketing origin from 3 to 12 pods
choices.resultTitle: Every click still crosses to origin
choices.resultBody: Twelve pods keep up at 45% CPU, but hit ratio is still 3%, visitors abroad pay a 250 ms round trip to origin, and you are paying for nine extra pods to render the same page 2.4 million times.

hints: Each click has a different URL, but do they get a different page?
Only one of the query parameters changes the response body.
The cache key does not have to be the whole URL.

incidents.title: Origin melts whenever a new trailer drops
incidents.brief: FlixNow posts a 40 MB trailer. Within a minute, cache servers across 280 CDN PoPs miss and each downloads it from origin, about 2,200 fetches. Origin CPU hits 94%; p95 is 6 s.
incidents.constraint: TTLs are already 24 hours and hit ratio is 97% once warm; only the cold-start fan-out hurts.
incidents.question: How do you stop every PoP hitting origin on the same miss?

choices.label: Enable a tiered origin shield in one region near origin
choices.resultTitle: One fetch per trailer reaches origin
choices.resultBody: PoPs now miss to a shield tier that coalesces concurrent requests, so origin serves each trailer once or twice instead of ~2,200 times, and its CPU drops to 25%. Cost: an extra hop of roughly 20-80 ms on cold misses from distant PoPs, plus a shield fee on the CDN bill.

choices.label: Script a pre-warm request to all 280 PoPs at publish
choices.resultBody: The script requests the trailer from all 280 PoPs at once, generating the same ~2,200 origin downloads five minutes earlier; origin CPU still peaks at 92%.

choices.label: Autoscale origin from 4 to 16 instances during launches
choices.resultBody: Sixteen instances absorb the ~2,200 PoP fetches and p95 falls from 6 s to 1.4 s. Origin egress still peaks near 12 Gbps on a 20 Gbps uplink, and every new video pulls the full fan-out again.

hints: Hit ratio is fine once warm; the problem is the first minute.
Count how many separate caches ask origin for the same new file.
A layer between the PoPs and origin could collapse those misses first.

incidents.title: Lagos shoppers wait 480 ms for every image
incidents.brief: MarketHub serves West Africa through a CDN whose nearest PoP is in Paris. Images hit the edge 95% of the time, but Lagos users still see 480 ms per image because each request travels about 5,000 km each way.
incidents.constraint: Nigeria is 30% of new signups; the origin in Frankfurt cannot move this quarter.
incidents.question: What brings images physically closer to Lagos?

choices.label: Add a CDN with Lagos PoPs, steered there by geo-DNS
choices.resultTitle: Images now ride a local hop
choices.resultBody: Geo-DNS sends Nigerian resolvers to a provider with PoPs in Lagos, so cache hits travel a few kilometres and image p95 falls from 480 to 60 ms. Cost: a second CDN contract, two configs to keep in sync, and a lower hit ratio while the new PoPs warm.

choices.label: Recompress every image at 60% JPEG quality
choices.resultBody: Images shrink by 40%, but they were only 80 KB; most of the 480 ms is round trips to Paris for DNS, TLS and the request itself. Latency drops to 430 ms and product photos now look blotchy.

choices.label: Stand up a second origin region in Johannesburg
choices.resultBody: Images were already served from the Paris edge, so a closer origin only speeds up the 5% of misses. Lagos users still reach the Paris PoP for every hit, and you now replicate the catalog to a second region.

hints: The hit ratio is 95%, so origin is rarely involved.
Measure the distance between the users and the cache that answers them.
Latency here is bound by round trips, not by bytes or compute.

incidents.title: 3.1 MB JavaScript bundle crawls on mobile
incidents.brief: TaskLane's app.[hash].js is cached at the edge with a 99% hit ratio, yet time-to-interactive on 3G is 9 s. The origin build writes plain JS and the CDN serves it uncompressed: 3.1 MB per first visit.
incidents.constraint: Engineering cannot rewrite the app or drop features this quarter.
incidents.question: What shrinks the bundle on the wire without touching app code?

choices.label: Serve Brotli-compressed bundles from the edge
choices.resultBody: The edge compresses the bundle once with Brotli and caches the encoded variant per Accept-Encoding, so browsers download about 620 KB instead of 3.1 MB and 3G time-to-interactive drops to 3.4 s. Cost: two cached variants per file (br and gzip for old clients) and a little edge CPU on the first miss.

choices.label: Split the bundle into 40 smaller chunks over HTTP/2
choices.resultBody: HTTP/2 multiplexes the 40 requests, but they still add up to 3.1 MB of uncompressed JavaScript because the app needs almost all of it at start. Time-to-interactive improves only to 7.6 s.

choices.label: Mark the bundle immutable with a one-year max-age
choices.resultBody: Returning visitors skip revalidation, but the slow metric is first visits, which still download 3.1 MB of plain text. The edge was already serving it at a 99% hit ratio.

hints: The file is cached; the problem is how many bytes cross the radio link.
Check the response's Content-Encoding header.
Text like JavaScript usually shrinks by 70-80% with the right encoding.

incidents.title: Price changes take an hour to reach shoppers
incidents.brief: GearBay caches product and category pages for 1 hour. When a price changes, the product also appears on about 3,000 category and search pages, and shoppers see the old price at checkout. 1,200 price changes happen daily.
incidents.constraint: Purge-all takes origin from 900 to 25,000 req/s, and pages must stay cached for at least an hour to keep origin small.
incidents.question: How do you refresh exactly the pages that show one product?

choices.label: Tag pages with product surrogate keys, then purge by tag
choices.resultBody: Origin sends a Surrogate-Key header listing every product on the page. A price change purges the tag product-8812, which drops just those ~3,000 pages worldwide in seconds while the other 2 million objects stay cached. Cost: origin must track which products each page renders.

choices.label: Trigger a full CDN purge whenever any price changes
choices.resultBody: Prices are right, but with 1,200 changes a day the cache is wiped roughly every 70 seconds. Hit ratio falls to 41% and origin sits at 97% CPU serving refills.

choices.label: Lower page TTL from one hour to 60 seconds
choices.resultBody: Old prices now last at most a minute, so mismatches fall to 30 an hour, but every one of the 2 million pages is refetched each minute it is viewed. Origin CPU climbs to 78%, breaking the one-hour constraint.

hints: The problem is not TTL length but knowing which cached pages mention a product.
A purge can target more than a URL or everything.
Let origin label each response with the entities it contains.

incidents.title: Thumbnail misses keep app servers at 90% CPU
incidents.brief: LearnGrid has 8 million course thumbnails (40 TB). Each PoP holds about 2 TB, so rarely viewed thumbnails are evicted within hours and hit ratio stalls at 70%. The 30% of misses are streamed from disk by the app servers.
incidents.constraint: The long tail is real: 60% of thumbnails are viewed less than once a day per region.
incidents.question: How do you stop misses from hurting the app tier?

choices.label: Make object storage the CDN origin for thumbnails
choices.resultBody: A /thumbs/* behavior points at the storage bucket, so the 15,000 misses/s are served by a service built for byte serving and app CPU drops to 35%. Hit ratio is still 70% because the tail is long, but a miss now costs ~80 ms from storage. Cost: bucket GET and egress fees.

choices.label: Raise thumbnail TTL from one day to one year
choices.resultBody: TTL is an upper bound, not a guarantee: the PoP's 2 TB cache still evicts cold thumbnails by LRU within hours. Hit ratio moves by one point and the app servers stay at 89% CPU.

choices.label: Pre-warm all 8 million thumbnails into every PoP
choices.resultBody: The warm-up job pulls 40 TB through the app servers into caches that hold 2 TB, so each PoP evicts what it just fetched. App CPU pins at 99% for the whole run and p95 hits 2.6 s.

hints: Compare the size of the library with the size of one PoP's cache.
Some misses are unavoidable here; ask who serves them.
Static bytes do not need an application server behind the CDN.

incidents.title: Personalized homepage drags 2 MB of CSS from origin
incidents.brief: FeedNest's homepage HTML is personalized per user, so the team set the whole domain to bypass the CDN. Every view pulls 2 MB of CSS, fonts and icons from origin in Virginia; Sydney users wait 3.4 s.
incidents.constraint: The HTML must never be shared between users; the CSS, fonts and icons are identical for everyone.
incidents.question: How do you cache the shared parts without leaking personal pages?

choices.label: Cache /static/* for a year; keep HTML no-store
choices.resultBody: A path rule caches /static/* at the edge with long TTLs and content-hashed names, while HTML stays private and uncached. Sydney loads the 2 MB locally and only the 40 KB HTML crosses the Pacific, so page load falls to 0.9 s. Cost: two cache behaviors to maintain and a build step for hashed names.

choices.label: Cache the homepage HTML for 60 seconds at the edge
choices.resultBody: Origin load collapses, but the edge now serves the first visitor's personalized HTML to everyone in that PoP for a minute. Screenshots of strangers' feeds hit social media within the hour.

choices.label: Inline all CSS and fonts into each HTML response
choices.resultBody: Inlining moves the 2 MB into the personalized HTML, so it can now never be cached, even by the browser. Every view re-downloads it from Virginia and origin CPU rises to 92% from rendering bigger pages.

hints: Only part of each response is personal.
A CDN can apply different rules to different paths on the same domain.
Separate the bytes everyone shares from the bytes one user owns.

incidents.title: Every video scrub is a round trip to origin
incidents.brief: ReelBox serves 6 GB 4K movie files. Players seek with HTTP Range requests, and the CDN is configured to pass ranges through uncached, so 14,000 range requests/s reach origin and seeks take 2.8 s.
incidents.constraint: The files are immutable after publish; re-encoding the 40,000-title catalog into a new format is out of scope this quarter.
incidents.question: How can the edge answer range requests from cache?

choices.label: Cache each file as fixed 8 MB slices at the edge
choices.resultBody: The edge maps each byte range to aligned 8 MB slices, fetches only missing slices from origin and caches them, so popular scenes are served locally and seek p95 drops to 180 ms. Cost: more cache objects per title and a small over-fetch when a range crosses a slice boundary.

choices.label: Fetch the full file into cache on any range miss
choices.resultBody: Each first range request makes the PoP pull the entire 6 GB movie before replying, so seeks on cold titles take nearly 10 s and origin egress spikes as hundreds of PoPs grab whole files for a few seconds of viewing.

choices.label: Disable Accept-Ranges so players stream files from the start
choices.resultBody: Without range support a player that jumps to minute 90 must download everything before it. Seeking effectively breaks, viewers abandon titles, and the few cached full files still do not help mid-movie starts.

hints: The files never change, so they are perfect cache candidates.
The trouble is that each request asks for a different piece of a huge file.
What if the cache stored the file as uniform pieces instead of all-or-nothing?

incidents.title: Origin drowns in 304 Not Modified replies
incidents.brief: DocuHub's static server sends ETags but no Cache-Control. The CDN treats assets as expired and revalidates every request: 22,000 conditional GETs/s reach origin, 99% answered 304, at 82% CPU.
incidents.constraint: The same CDN account also fronts /api/*, which returns per-user data.
incidents.question: How do you let the edge serve assets without asking origin each time?

choices.label: Send Cache-Control max-age=86400 on /static responses
choices.resultBody: With an explicit day-long max-age the edge serves assets from cache and revalidates each one about once a day, so origin requests fall from 22,000 to roughly 600/s and p95 drops to 35 ms. Cost: an asset changed without renaming can be stale for up to a day, so hashed filenames matter.

choices.label: Make ETags cheaper with a precomputed hash per file
choices.resultBody: Each 304 costs less CPU, so origin drops to 64%, but every request still waits for a round trip to origin before the edge answers. The count of conditional GETs is unchanged.

choices.label: Force a 10-minute edge TTL for every path in the account
choices.resultBody: Assets cache nicely, but the rule also caches /api/* responses, so users in the same PoP receive each other's account JSON for up to ten minutes. Security opens an incident.

hints: Almost every origin reply is a 304, so the content is not changing.
Without a freshness lifetime, a cache must check with origin before reusing a copy.
Tell the edge how long the copy stays fresh, only for the paths that are shared.

incidents.title: Product images drop to a 4% edge hit ratio
incidents.brief: ShopNest's CDN hit ratio for /img/* fell from 95% to 4% after analytics set a per-visitor cookie site-wide. The CDN keys on Cookie, so origin now serves 18,000 image req/s.
incidents.constraint: Images are public and identical for everyone; the analytics cookie must stay on HTML pages.
incidents.question: What restores the edge hit ratio for images?

choices.label: Strip cookies from the /img/* cache key at the edge
choices.resultBody: The edge now ignores and removes Cookie for /img/*, so one cached copy serves every visitor; hit ratio returns to 95% and origin drops to about 900 req/s. Cost: nothing under /img/* can use cookies for per-user logic, and the edge rule must track origin route changes.

choices.label: Raise image TTL from 1 day to 30 days at the edge
choices.resultTitle: Longer TTL, still one copy per visitor
choices.resultBody: Each visitor's cookie still creates a unique cache entry, so entries live longer but are never reused; hit ratio stays near 5% while edge storage churns.

choices.label: Double origin image servers and add a Redis thumbnail cache
choices.resultTitle: Origin propped up, edge still bypassed
choices.resultBody: Origin copes at 50% CPU, but every image still travels from origin with ~150 ms extra latency, egress costs climb, and the edge hit ratio stays at 4%.

hints: Hit ratio fell on the day a new cookie appeared.
Look at what the CDN uses to decide whether two requests are the same object.
Public images don't need anything per-visitor in their cache key.

incidents.title: One CSS typo fix spiked origin worldwide
incidents.brief: An engineer fixed a typo in site.css and ran 'purge all'. 2.1 million cached objects were dropped; origin jumped from 800 to 26,000 req/s and 97% CPU for 20 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Designers ship CSS fixes several times a day, and each fix must reach visitors within a minute.
incidents.question: How should a single-file fix reach users next time?

choices.label: Ship content-hashed filenames with immutable TTLs
choices.resultBody: Builds now emit site.3f9a1c.css and the HTML, cached for 60 s, points at the new name, so visitors get the fix within a minute while the other 2.1 million objects stay cached. Cost: a build step that rewrites references, and old hashed files must stay at origin until cached HTML expires.

choices.label: Purge only site.css by URL, keeping the same filename
choices.resultBody: The single-URL purge spares origin, but browsers already hold site.css under a 1-day max-age, which no CDN purge can reach; most returning visitors keep the typo until tomorrow.

choices.label: Set every asset's TTL to 60 seconds so fixes appear
choices.resultBody: Fixes now appear within a minute, but 2.1 million objects revalidate every 60 s; origin settles at 14,000 req/s and 80% CPU all day, not just after a purge.

hints: Only one of 2.1 million objects actually changed.
Browsers cache the file too, and a CDN purge can't reach them.
If the fixed file had a new name, nothing would need purging.

incidents.title: Anonymous catalog API pins origin at 88% CPU
incidents.brief: SnackRun's mobile app calls GET /v2/catalog on every launch: 35,000 req/s worldwide, all to origin in Oregon. The JSON is the same for every anonymous user and changes about every 5 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Prices shown in the catalog must be at most 5 minutes old, and launches abroad already take 1.2 s.
incidents.question: How do you serve the catalog without origin handling every launch?

choices.label: Edge-cache the catalog JSON with stale-while-revalidate
choices.resultTitle: One refresh per PoP every 4 minutes
choices.resultBody: Each PoP keeps the JSON for 240 s and refreshes it in the background with stale-while-revalidate, so origin sees a few hundred req/s instead of 35,000 and launches abroad take 70 ms. Worst-case age stays under 5 minutes. Cost: authenticated variants must stay uncached.

choices.label: Cache the catalog JSON in Redis next to the API
choices.resultTitle: The database relaxes, the API does not
choices.resultBody: The catalog DB is spared, but all 35,000 requests/s still cross oceans to Oregon and pass through the API tier for TLS, routing and serialization. CPU falls to 55% and far-away launches still take a second.

choices.label: Cache the catalog JSON on each phone for 5 minutes
choices.resultBody: Most launches come from users who have not opened the app in over 5 minutes, so the on-device cache is usually empty. Origin load drops only about 10% and first-launch latency is unchanged.

hints: The response is identical for every anonymous user.
Dynamic does not mean uncacheable; the data tolerates a few minutes of age.
Shared caches honor a separate max-age and can refresh in the background.

incidents.title: São Paulo checkout waits 900 ms before the first byte
incidents.brief: CartPilot's personalized checkout API runs only in Virginia. Brazilian users open a new TCP and TLS connection to it on each visit: three round trips of 130 ms before any data, plus the request itself.
incidents.constraint: Checkout responses are per user and must never be cached.
incidents.question: How do you cut round trips for traffic the CDN cannot cache?

choices.label: Terminate TLS at São Paulo PoPs, pooled links to origin
choices.resultBody: The TCP and TLS handshakes now complete with a PoP 10 ms away, and the PoP forwards the request over already-open, pooled connections to Virginia, so only one 130 ms round trip remains and TTFB p95 falls to 320 ms. Nothing is cached. Cost: CDN request fees on dynamic traffic.

choices.label: Cache checkout responses at the edge for 60 seconds
choices.resultBody: Latency looks great, but the edge replays one user's checkout page to others in the same PoP, including names and addresses. The rule is rolled back after the first privacy complaint.

choices.label: Switch the origin certificate to ECDSA for faster handshakes
choices.resultBody: ECDSA trims server CPU per handshake, but the delay is the 130 ms trips across the equator, not signing time. TTFB drops by about 20 ms.

hints: Count the round trips before the first byte of the response.
A CDN can speed up traffic it never caches.
Move the handshake close to the user and keep the long-haul connection open.

incidents.title: An 'Oops' page outlives the outage by an hour
incidents.brief: TicketNow's origin failed for 4 minutes. Its error handler returned 'Something went wrong' with HTTP 200 and the default Cache-Control max-age=3600, so the CDN cached it on 1,800 event pages. Origin is healthy; users still see errors.
incidents.constraint: Event pages must keep their one-hour TTL; the on-sale traffic of 60,000 req/s depends on it.
incidents.question: Now what stops the next failure from being cached as a good page?

choices.label: Return a real 503 with no-store from the error handler
choices.resultTitle: Failures are never mistaken for pages
choices.resultBody: After a one-time purge of the poisoned pages, the handler now returns 503 with Cache-Control: no-store, so the CDN never stores failures and can fall back to stale content or retry. Future outages clear the moment origin recovers. Cost: the error path needs its own tests and monitoring.

choices.label: Add a runbook step to purge the whole CDN after outages
choices.resultBody: Someone has to notice and run it, so errors linger for 10-20 minutes each time, and purging everything during an on-sale sends all 60,000 req/s to origin at once, pushing it to 96% CPU.

choices.label: Cut the event page TTL from 1 hour to 30 seconds
choices.resultBody: Cached errors now expire within 30 seconds, but every event page is refetched twice a minute per PoP, violating the TTL constraint and driving origin to 91% CPU during on-sales.

hints: The CDN did exactly what the headers told it to.
Look at the status code and caching headers of the error response.
A cache decides what to store from the response's status and Cache-Control.

mitigation.question: Fans are seeing a cached 'Oops' page on 1,800 events. What do you do first?

choices.label: Purge only the 1,800 event pages that cached the error
choices.resultBody: The 1,800 poisoned pages drop from every PoP in seconds and refill from the healthy origin, which peaks at 38% CPU. Errors fall to near zero, but the handler will still cache its next failure.

choices.label: Purge the whole CDN so every page refetches from origin
choices.resultTitle: On-sale traffic hits origin at once
choices.resultBody: All 60,000 req/s miss together in the middle of the on-sale. Origin hits 97% CPU and starts timing out, and some refills cache the error page all over again.

choices.label: Restart the ticket origin pods to clear the error state
choices.resultBody: Origin had recovered minutes ago, so the restart changes nothing at the edge: 1,800 pages keep serving the cached error until their hour runs out.

incidents.title: Leaked lecture links keep playing for a week
incidents.brief: EduVault signs lecture URLs for 1 hour, but the CDN ignores the signature and caches each video as public for 7 days. One leaked link has served 48,000 views to non-students.
incidents.constraint: Hit ratio must stay above 90%: the 4K lectures cost about $0.08/GB to serve from origin.
incidents.question: How do you keep lectures cached but authorized?

choices.label: Verify the signed token at the edge, not in the key
choices.resultBody: Each PoP verifies the signature and 1-hour expiry before serving, so the leaked link returns 403 once it expires, while the cache key ignores the token and all students share one copy; hit ratio stays at 96%. Cost: signing-key rotation and clock skew to manage, and a leaked link still works until its hour runs out.

choices.label: Include the signature query string in the CDN cache key
choices.resultBody: The leaked URL's signature is now its own cache entry with a 7-day TTL, so it keeps playing from the edge; meanwhile every student's unique URL misses, hit ratio falls to 9%, and origin CPU hits 85%.

choices.label: Mark lecture videos Cache-Control: private, no-store
choices.resultTitle: Authorized, but origin takes every byte
choices.resultBody: The CDN stops caching lectures; unauthorized plays end because origin checks tokens, but 9,000 req/s of 4K video now stream from origin at 96% CPU with a 2.4 s p95.

hints: The CDN is treating a private object like a public one.
Two jobs are tangled: deciding who may watch, and deciding which bytes to reuse.
The edge can check a signature without making it part of the object's identity.

incidents.title: Users stuck on last week's app for seven days
incidents.brief: PlanIt's SPA serves index.html with max-age=604800. After a deploy, users load the old shell, which requests JS chunks that no longer exist; 6% of sessions crash with ChunkLoadError.
incidents.constraint: The hashed JS and CSS files are fine with a one-year TTL; the entry URL must stay /.
incidents.question: How should the entry HTML be cached?

choices.label: Serve index.html as no-cache with ETag revalidation
choices.resultTitle: The shell checks in on every load
choices.resultBody: Browsers and the edge may store index.html but must revalidate it each time, getting a tiny 304 until a deploy changes the ETag, then the new 2 KB shell. Hashed chunks keep their one-year TTL. Cost: one small conditional request per page load.

choices.label: Purge index.html from the CDN after each deploy
choices.resultTitle: The edge is fresh, browsers are not
choices.resultBody: The purge clears the CDN, but returning users never ask the CDN: their browsers hold index.html for up to 7 days under max-age. Crashes fall only slightly, from new visitors getting the fresh shell.

choices.label: Give index.html a hashed name like the JS chunks
choices.resultTitle: Nobody can find the new name
choices.resultBody: The entry point is whatever users type or bookmark, which is /. A hashed HTML name would need something else, cached briefly, to point at it, so the stale / copy keeps serving the old shell.

hints: The hashed files are fine; only one file has a URL that never changes.
A CDN purge cannot reach a browser's own cache.
Stable URLs need short lifetimes or revalidation; hashed URLs can live forever.

incidents.title: Origin outage takes the whole news site down
incidents.brief: DailyWire's origin database failed for 12 minutes. Article pages have a 60 s TTL, so within a minute nearly all 50,000 req/s at the CDN became 502s, though every article had been cached moments earlier.
incidents.constraint: Breaking-news pages must refresh within 60 seconds whenever origin is healthy.
incidents.question: How do you keep serving readers while origin is down?

choices.label: Serve expired copies via stale-if-error while origin fails
choices.resultBody: With max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=86400, the edge keeps serving the last good copy whenever origin returns 5xx, so errors fall to about 1% (pages never cached). Cost: during an outage readers may see articles up to 12 minutes old, so pages should show an 'updated at' time.

choices.label: Raise the article TTL from 60 seconds to 1 hour
choices.resultBody: The next outage is masked, but breaking-news corrections now take up to an hour to reach readers, breaking the 60-second freshness rule every normal day.

choices.label: Make the CDN retry origin three times before returning 502
choices.resultTitle: Retries tripled load on a dead origin
choices.resultBody: Each miss now hits the failing origin three times, so it sees about 150,000 req/s instead of 50,000; recovery takes 4 minutes longer and readers still get 502s, after an 8 s wait.

hints: Every article was cached a minute before the outage.
The edge threw away copies it still had because they were past their TTL.
Cache-Control can say how long an expired copy may still be used when origin fails.

incidents.title: Image misses slow down a little more every hour
incidents.brief: PixelPort's CDN misses hit 12 image-resizer VMs. Since Monday's libvips upgrade, each process leaks about 300 MB an hour; after 20 hours VMs start swapping and miss p95 climbs from 200 ms to 4 s.
incidents.constraint: Patched libvips ships Thursday, in three days; rolling back reopens a CVE, so the leaky build stays until then.
incidents.question: What keeps CDN misses fast until the patch ships?

choices.label: Rolling restart of the resizer VMs every 12 hours

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A scheduled restart bridges a known leak for three days; it is a mitigation with an end date, not a fix.

choices.resultTitle: Memory resets before it can swap
choices.resultBody: A cron job drains and restarts two VMs at a time behind the load balancer, so no process lives past 12 hours and none reaches the 20-hour swap point. Miss p95 returns to 200 ms. Cost: a restart job to delete on Thursday, and a leak that would return if the patch slips.

choices.label: Put an origin shield in front of the resizer fleet
choices.resultBody: The shield coalesces duplicate misses from different PoPs and cuts resizer traffic by about 30%. The leak grows with every resize, so VMs now start swapping around hour 28 instead of hour 20, and p95 still reaches seconds before Thursday.

choices.label: Pre-render every image variant into object storage
choices.resultTitle: A two-week backfill for a three-day bug
choices.resultBody: Rendering every master into every width and format runs on the same leaking resizers, pushing them to 95% CPU and swapping sooner. The backfill needs about two weeks, so it finishes long after Thursday's patch removes the leak anyway.

hints: The slowdown tracks process uptime, not traffic.
A fresh resizer process is fast for its first 20 hours.
The real fix is already scheduled; you only have to bridge three days.

incidents.title: 4K premiere saturates the origin uplink
incidents.brief: Autoscaling carried Tuesday's trailer. Friday's 4K premiere is 160 MB; about 2,200 PoP fetches push origin egress to the 20 Gbps uplink cap, and misses time out across 280 PoPs.
incidents.constraint: The uplink can't be upgraded before next quarter, and instance CPU is only 55%.
incidents.question: What keeps the next premiere under the uplink cap?

choices.label: Send PoP misses through a shield tier that coalesces
choices.resultTitle: One fetch per premiere reaches origin
choices.resultBody: Misses from all 280 PoPs now funnel through one shield that fetches each video once or twice, so origin egress drops from 20 Gbps to under 1 Gbps. Cost: a shield fee and 20–80 ms extra on cold misses from distant PoPs.

choices.label: Autoscale origin to 32 instances before each premiere
choices.resultBody: Thirty-two instances idle at 28% CPU, but they share the same 20 Gbps uplink, so the 2,200 fetches still queue on the wire and misses keep timing out.

choices.label: Raise the CDN origin timeout from 10 s to 60 s
choices.resultBody: Fewer fetches abort, but each one now holds a connection for up to 60 s on a full uplink. Open connections triple and p95 climbs from 9 s to 24 s.

hints: CPU is at 55%; look at the wire, not the cores.
Count origin fetches per new video: roughly one per PoP cache server.
What could make 280 PoPs ask origin once instead of 2,200 times?

incidents.title: Image transform bill triples in a week
incidents.brief: Edge resizing accepts any ?w= value. Clients now request 1,400 distinct widths per image, so the edge hit ratio fell from 93% to 58% and transform fees tripled to $1,800 a month.
incidents.constraint: Phones need sharp images near their real width; the site's layout uses five breakpoints.
incidents.question: How do you stop every width becoming its own cached variant?

choices.label: Round requested widths up to eight fixed sizes at the edge
choices.resultBody: The edge snaps ?w= to 8 widths from 320 to 1920 px and serves the next size up, so each image has 8 variants per format. Hit ratio returns to 92% and transform fees fall to about $700. Cost: phones download up to ~20% more pixels than they display.

choices.label: Buy more edge storage so every width variant stays cached
choices.resultBody: Storage wasn't the limit: most of the 1,400 widths are requested once or twice per TTL, so they miss regardless of disk size. Hit ratio edges up to 61% and you pay for the storage too.

choices.label: Move resizing back to origin and cache the results there
choices.resultBody: Transform fees leave the CDN bill, but each of the 1,400 widths is still a distinct URL, so edge misses stay at 42% and each now waits on origin CPU. p95 rises to 3.4 s.

hints: Count the distinct URLs per image, not the images.
A cache can only reuse a variant when two phones ask for exactly the same one.
How many sizes does a five-breakpoint layout actually need?

incidents.title: Bulk price import empties the edge
incidents.brief: A supplier import changed 40,000 prices in 3 minutes, firing 40,000 tag purges. Pages drop faster than they refill: hit ratio fell from 95% to 30% and origin is at 94% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Changed prices must still reach shoppers within a minute.
incidents.question: How do you keep bulk updates from flattening the cache?

choices.label: Soft-purge by tag and refresh stale pages in the background
choices.resultBody: Purged pages are marked stale instead of dropped: the next request gets the old copy while one background fetch per PoP refreshes it, so origin sees a steady trickle instead of a wall. Hit ratio stays at 93% and prices update within ~30 s. Cost: one request per page may still see the old price.

choices.label: Queue tag purges and release at most 50 per second
choices.resultBody: Origin stays calm, but 40,000 purges at 50 per second take over 13 minutes to drain, so most changed prices stay wrong far past the one-minute rule and checkout mismatches jump.

choices.label: Autoscale the catalog origin to absorb each import's refill
choices.resultBody: Origin copes at 60% CPU, but the edge is still emptied by every import: hit ratio sits at 30% for 20 minutes and shoppers far from Virginia wait 900 ms per page.

hints: The purges aren't wrong; losing the cached copy is.
A dropped object costs a full miss; a stale object can still be served once.
What if purged pages were marked old instead of deleted?
